common_name: Judith Hindle Pitcher Plant (Variegated Pink-White Sarracenia)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes and set into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss; never use fertilized potting mix or garden soil, and keep the pot sitting in a tray of rain water or distilled water at all times.

directions: Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water. Judith Hindle is a classic, widely grown Sarracenia hybrid whose tall, trumpet-shaped pitchers open pale cream-white heavily veined in soft pink and mature toward a deeper rose blush, one of the most delicately colored pitcher plant hybrids commonly available. Like other Sarracenia it traps insects that slip down the waxy inner pitcher walls, providing nutrients the nutrient-poor bog soil cannot. Give it full sun for the strongest pitcher color and production, and allow the plant a natural winter dormancy with reduced water and shorter days, since Sarracenia requires this cold rest to remain healthy long-term.

common_name: Dana's Delight Pitcher Plant (Yellow-Green Sarracenia Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes and set into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss; never use fertilized potting mix or garden soil, and keep the pot sitting in a tray of rain water or distilled water at all times.

directions: Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water. Dana's Delight produces tall, slender, upright pitchers in bright chartreuse-yellow to lime green with fine reddish veining near the hood, a fresh, luminous color combination distinct from the deeper reds and purples of many other Sarracenia hybrids. As with other pitcher plants, insects are drawn to nectar at the pitcher rim, slip down the waxy inner walls, and are digested to supply nutrients the poor bog soil lacks. Give it full sun for the strongest pitcher color and production, and allow a natural winter dormancy with reduced water and shorter days, since Sarracenia requires this cold rest to remain healthy long-term.

common_name: Adrian Slack Pitcher Plant (Red-Veined Sarracenia Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes and set into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss; never use fertilized potting mix or garden soil, and keep the pot sitting in a tray of rain water or distilled water at all times.

directions: Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water. Adrian Slack, named for the British carnivorous plant grower and author who helped popularize Sarracenia cultivation, produces tall pitchers with a pale green to cream body overlaid by a dense network of dark red veining that intensifies toward the flaring hood, a bold, high-contrast pattern prized by pitcher plant collectors. As with other Sarracenia it traps insects that slip down the waxy inner pitcher walls, supplying nutrients the nutrient-poor bog soil cannot provide. Give it full sun for the strongest pitcher color and production, and allow a natural winter dormancy with reduced water and shorter days, since Sarracenia requires this cold rest to remain healthy long-term.

common_name: Miranda Pitcher Plant (Large Easy-Growing Nepenthes Hybrid)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or pot up nursery starts in spring into a well-draining mix of sphagnum moss and orchid bark or perlite; keep the medium moist year-round with pure distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater and provide bright, above-average humidity.

directions: Grow in a well-draining mix of sphagnum moss and orchid bark or perlite in bright, filtered light with above-average humidity, watering only with distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rain water. Miranda is one of the most widely grown Nepenthes hybrids for its combination of vigorous growth, tolerance of average home humidity, and large, showy pitchers in mottled red-orange over a cream to yellow base, considerably bigger and more colorful than many beginner-friendly Nepenthes. It climbs readily as it matures, producing both lower ground pitchers and, later, differently shaped upper pitchers on the same vine. Provide a hanging basket or elevated position to display the dangling pitchers, and feed occasionally with a small live or dead insect if grown fully indoors away from natural prey.

common_name: Bloody Mary Pitcher Plant (Dark Red Nepenthes Hybrid)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or pot up nursery starts in spring into a well-draining mix of sphagnum moss and orchid bark or perlite; keep the medium moist year-round with pure distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rainwater and provide bright, above-average humidity.

directions: Grow in a well-draining mix of sphagnum moss and orchid bark or perlite in bright, filtered light with above-average humidity, watering only with distilled, reverse-osmosis, or rain water. Bloody Mary produces pitchers in an intensely saturated dark red to near-maroon color with darker speckling, among the darkest coloring available in commonly grown Nepenthes hybrids, giving it a dramatic, moody presence distinct from the greens, oranges, and pale pinks of most pitcher plant hybrids. It climbs as it matures, producing lower ground pitchers followed by upper pitchers with a different shape on the same vine. Provide a hanging basket or elevated position to display the dangling pitchers, and feed occasionally with a small live or dead insect if grown fully indoors away from natural prey.
